keyVerseText: And Aram begat Aminadab; and Aminadab begat Naasson; and Naasson begat Salmon;
rootMeaning: The name Σαλμών (Salmṓn) originates from the Hebrew שַׂלְמוֹן (Salmôwn), which is related to the word שַׂלְמָה meaning 'garment.' This suggests that the name carries connotations of clothing or covering, which may symbolically point to protection or honor. Thus, beyond simply being a proper name, the root sense enriches our understanding by hinting at a person who may represent a covering or a significant role within a family lineage.
usageInScripture: The word Σαλμών appears three times in the New Testament, consistently translated as 'Salmon,' identifying an Israelite ancestor in the genealogy of Jesus. Twice it is rendered simply as 'Salmon,' and once in a phrase indicating lineage, 'which was the son of Salmon.' This consistency in translation underscores the importance of Salmon as a historical figure within the biblical genealogical record, emphasizing his role as a link in the messianic line.
theologicalSignificance: Understanding Σαλμών as a name rooted in the idea of a 'garment' invites reflection on how God providentially weaves individuals into His redemptive plan. Salmon, as an ancestor of David and ultimately of Christ, symbolizes how God covers and upholds His covenant people through generations. His presence in Scripture highlights the faithfulness of God's promises and the continuity of salvation history, reminding believers that Christ's coming was part of a divinely ordained lineage. This reinforces the biblical truth that God works through ordinary people and family lines to accomplish His extraordinary purposes.
keyVerseReflection: Matthew 1:4 states, 'And Aram begat Aminadab; and Aminadab begat Naasson; and Naasson begat Salmon;' placing Salmon firmly within the genealogy of Jesus. The mention of Salmon here is more than a historical note; it marks the continuation of God's covenantal promise through a tangible human lineage. Salmon's inclusion affirms the reality of Christ's human ancestry, grounding the Savior's identity in history and fulfilling the Old Testament prophecies about the Messiah's descent.
